triage.name: Pneumonia
triage.reason: Core undifferentiated fever and respiratory complaint with clear diagnosis by history, exam and imaging; rich severity and differential teaching.

age.peak: bimodal: children under 5 and adults over 65

demographics: More common and more severe at the extremes of age
Slightly more common in males overall
More common in Black, American Indian and Alaska Native adults than in White adults in the US

risk_factors.text: Cigarette smoking or secondhand smoke exposure
Recent viral upper respiratory infection or influenza
Difficulty coughing or swallowing (stroke, dementia, neuromuscular disease)
Residence in a nursing home or long-term care facility
Exposure to contaminated water systems or air conditioning (Legionella)
Exposure to birds or bird droppings
Occupational exposure to toxic fumes, chemicals or pollutants

comorbidities: Stroke or other cause of dysphagia
HIV infection or other immunocompromising condition
Solid organ or stem cell transplant
social_history: Residence in a long-term care facility
Recent travel with hotel or cruise ship stay (Legionella)
Exposure to children in daycare or school
exposures: Influenza or other circulating respiratory virus
Contaminated water aerosols (showers, hot tubs, cooling towers)
Recent dental work or aspiration event

chief_complaints.text: I've been coughing up green stuff for a few days
I feel like I can't catch my breath
It hurts when I take a deep breath
I've had a fever and chills
I feel really tired and achy

hpi.onset: Subacute, over 1–3 days; often follows a few days of a cold or flu-like illness
hpi.progression: Starts as a dry or mildly productive cough with low-grade fever, then worsens over 1–3 days with higher fever, more purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath
hpi.location: Chest, often one side; may be described as under the shoulder blade or in the lower chest
hpi.radiation: Pleuritic pain may radiate to the shoulder or upper abdomen
hpi.quality: Cough is wet and productive; chest pain is sharp and stabbing with breathing
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; fever 101–103°F, cough and dyspnea interfere with sleep and daily activity
hpi.timing: Continuous symptoms; fever may spike in the evening; chest pain is worse with each breath

associated_symptoms.text: Productive cough with yellow, green or rust-colored sputum
Pleuritic chest pain with breathing or coughing

pertinent_negatives: Cough lasting more than 3 weeks before this illness
Weight loss or night sweats for weeks
Recent travel to a tuberculosis-endemic country
Known HIV infection or other severe immunosuppression
Recent hospitalization or antibiotic use within 90 days
Pleuritic pain that started suddenly with breathlessness in a postoperative or immobilized patient
Unilateral leg swelling or calf pain
Recurrent episodes of pneumonia in the same lobe

argues_against: Sudden onset pleuritic pain with breathlessness in an immobilized patient (pulmonary embolism)
Chronic cough with weight loss and hemoptysis (tuberculosis or malignancy)
Exertional chest pressure relieved by rest (acute coronary syndrome)
Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (heart failure)
Confusion with neck stiffness and photophobia (meningitis)

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls or general decline rather than fever and cough; fever may be absent or temperature may be lower than normal, and the chest exam can be unimpressive despite significant infection.
Infants may show no specific signs; they can be irritable, lethargic, feed poorly, vomit or have a fever without a clear source.
Children often have fever, tachypnea and cough but may not produce sputum; abdominal pain or vomiting can be prominent, and wheezing may be heard.

Symptoms may be milder or more prolonged, fever may be blunted, and opportunistic organisms such as Pneumocystis, fungi or mycobacteria should be considered; presentation can be insidious with dry cough and progressive dyspnea.
Presentation is similar to non-pregnant adults, but dyspnea and fatigue are common in normal pregnancy and may delay recognition; physiologic changes can make hypoxemia develop faster.
missing_classic_features: Clear distinction of dyspnea from normal pregnancy

atypical.how_it_differs: May have more severe illness and higher risk of bacteremia; fever and symptoms can be blunted, and hyperglycemia may worsen.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable at rest, no distress; may appear mildly fatigued
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, flushed, prefers sitting upright, speaks in short sentences
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, using accessory muscles, tripod positioning
general.critical: Lethargic or confused, pale or mottled, unable to speak in full sentences, may be obtunded

findings.maneuver: Observe the respiratory rate and pattern at rest
Observe for use of neck and intercostal muscles and supraclavicular retractions
findings.finding: Accessory muscle recruitment, nasal flaring or retractions

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and level of alertness
Auscultate all lung fields with the stethoscope
findings.finding: Focal inspiratory crackles over the affected lobe

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the area of consolidation
findings.finding: Bronchial breath sounds with increased transmission of voice sounds

findings.maneuver: Percuss the posterior and lateral chest walls
findings.finding: Focal dullness over the consolidated area

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to say 'E' while auscultating over the area of consolidation
Palpate the chest while the patient repeats '99'
findings.finding: Increased tactile fremitus over the affected area

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the area of pleuritic pain
Percuss the lung bases and assess for decreased breath sounds
findings.finding: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds suggesting pleural effusion

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate the precordium
findings.finding: No murmur, rub or gallop; normal S1 and S2

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck veins at 45 degrees

findings.finding: No unilateral calf swelling or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for rash or petechiae

labs.caveat: A normal or low white count does not rule out pneumonia and can be seen in older adults or overwhelming sepsis.
A left shift supports bacterial infection but is not specific.
Relative lymphopenia is common with acute bacterial infection; lymphocytosis suggests a viral cause.
Elevated BUN is part of the CURB-65 severity score and may reflect dehydration or renal injury.
Rising creatinine suggests dehydration, sepsis or acute kidney injury and guides antibiotic dosing.
Hyponatremia is common in Legionella pneumonia and can occur with SIADH.
Elevated lactate indicates hypoperfusion and possible sepsis; it is not specific to pneumonia.
Supports a bacterial cause and can guide antibiotic duration, but should not be used alone to withhold antibiotics in a sick patient.
Rises with inflammation of any cause; useful for tracking response but not for diagnosis alone.
Acidemia on ABG indicates respiratory failure or severe sepsis.
Rising PaCO2 suggests fatigue and impending respiratory failure.
Hypoxemia out of proportion to the chest x-ray can suggest Pneumocystis pneumonia.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before obtaining a chest x-ray or CT.

findings.finding: New atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

imaging.preferred_when: Initial imaging in all patients with suspected pneumonia

findings.text: Lobar or segmental airspace opacity with air bronchograms
Normal chest x-ray early in the illness or in dehydrated patients

imaging.preferred_when: Complicated or nonresolving pneumonia, suspicion of abscess, empyema or an underlying structural lung disease

findings.text: Centrilobular nodules or tree-in-bud opacities suggesting aspiration or atypical infection

imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy, children, or bedside assessment when x-ray is unavailable or nondiagnostic

initial.why: Assesses leukocytosis and left shift supporting infection
Evaluates hydration, renal function and sodium; BUN is part of CURB-65
Confirms the diagnosis and defines the extent of consolidation
Detects hypoxemia and guides oxygen therapy
Rules out pregnancy before chest x-ray

supporting.only_if: severe disease, immunocompromised, or suspected bacteremia
severe disease, treatment failure, or suspected drug-resistant organism

supporting.test: urine antigen tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella
supporting.why: Rapid identification of common bacterial causes
supporting.only_if: severe community-acquired pneumonia or epidemiologic clues

supporting.why: Detects influenza and allows antiviral therapy
supporting.only_if: influenza is circulating or the patient has influenza-like illness

supporting.why: Detects COVID-19 and guides isolation and antiviral therapy
Supports bacterial infection and can guide antibiotic duration
supporting.only_if: diagnostic uncertainty about bacterial versus viral cause
hypotension, tachycardia or concern for sepsis

supporting.why: Assesses oxygenation and ventilation in severe disease
supporting.only_if: severe hypoxemia, respiratory distress or impending failure
suspected abscess, empyema or failure to improve

supporting.why: Avoids radiation and can be done at the bedside

not_indicated.why: No role in diagnosing pneumonia; may be elevated nonspecifically
Not routinely needed unless acute coronary syndrome is suspected
Not routinely needed unless heart failure is suspected
Not routinely needed unless urinary symptoms or sepsis of unclear source

decision_points: Pregnancy test before chest x-ray or CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Use CURB-65 or PSI to decide inpatient versus outpatient care
Blood and sputum cultures before antibiotics in severe disease
Consider tuberculosis and fungal infection in nonresolving or cavitary pneumonia
Escalate to CT when the patient fails to improve or complications are suspected

criteria.name: CURB-65
criteria.summary: Severity score for community-acquired pneumonia using confusion, urea (BUN), respiratory rate, blood pressure and age 65 or older; higher scores predict mortality and guide site of care.
items: Systolic BP < 90 or diastolic BP ≤ 60 mm Hg

criteria.name: Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)
criteria.summary: Validated risk score using demographics, comorbidities, exam and lab findings to stratify mortality risk and identify low-risk patients suitable for outpatient treatment.

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia can mimic pneumonia, and both can cause hypoxemia and low-grade fever.
differential.trigger: Sudden-onset dyspnea or pleuritic pain in an immobilized, postoperative, pregnant or cancer patient, or unilateral leg swelling.

history: Abrupt onset over seconds to minutes rather than days
Recent surgery, immobilization, long travel or active cancer
Prior venous thromboembolism
Hemoptysis may occur but sputum is not purulent
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
Unilateral calf swelling or tenderness
Clear lungs on auscultation despite marked dyspnea
Signs of right heart strain (elevated JVP, loud P2)
labs: D-dimer elevated (useful only to rule out in low-risk patients)
PaO2 low with a widened alveolar-arterial gradient
WBC usually normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: Chest x-ray often normal or shows focal oligemia, not consolidation
CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defect in a pulmonary artery
Lower extremity ultrasound may show a deep vein thrombus
ecg: S1Q3T3 pattern, right axis deviation or new right bundle branch block

differential.name: Acute decompensated heart failure
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea, crackles, hypoxemia and chest x-ray opacities overlap with pneumonia, especially in older adults.
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, weight gain or leg swelling in a patient with known cardiac disease.

history: Progressive dyspnea over days to weeks with orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Weight gain and peripheral edema
No fever or productive cough
Known heart failure, coronary disease or valvular disease
exam: Bilateral basilar crackles rather than focal findings
Elevated jugular venous pressure
S3 gallop
Bilateral pitting leg edema
labs: May have hyponatremia and elevated creatinine
imaging: Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, Kerley B lines and pleural effusions
Bilateral, symmetric interstitial or alveolar edema rather than a focal lobar opacity
ecg: May show prior infarction, left ventricular hypertrophy or atrial fibrillation

differential.name: Acute bronchitis
differential.why_considered: Cough with sputum, low-grade fever and malaise is the most common mimic and is frequently mistaken for pneumonia.

history: Cough often dry or minimally productive, lasting days to weeks
Fever absent or low grade
No pleuritic chest pain or significant dyspnea
Often follows a viral upper respiratory infection
exam: Lungs clear or diffuse wheezes without focal crackles
No dullness, egophony or bronchial breath sounds
Normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation

differential.name: Tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Cough, fever, night sweats and lung opacities can resemble pneumonia, particularly in the upper lobes or in endemic settings.
differential.trigger: Subacute or chronic cough with weight loss, night sweats, hemoptysis, or upper-lobe or cavitary disease.

history: Weeks to months of cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss
Hemoptysis
Birth or residence in a tuberculosis-endemic country
Known exposure, incarceration or homelessness
HIV infection or other immunosuppression
exam: Cachexia and chronic illness appearance
Upper-lobe crackles or amphoric breath sounds with cavitation
Lymphadenopathy
labs: Interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test positive
Sputum nucleic acid amplification test positive
imaging: Upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, fibrosis or miliary pattern
Chest x-ray changes that do not resolve with antibiotics

differential.name: Lung cancer
differential.why_considered: Can present with cough, hemoptysis and a focal opacity, and may cause post-obstructive pneumonia that fails to clear.
differential.trigger: Pneumonia that does not resolve, recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe, or weight loss and hemoptysis in a smoker.

history: Cough and hemoptysis over weeks to months
Unintentional weight loss and anorexia
Long smoking history or occupational exposure
Recurrent pneumonia in the same location
exam: Focal wheeze or diminished breath sounds from endobronchial obstruction
Hoarseness, Horner syndrome or superior vena cava syndrome
Clubbing or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
labs: No leukocytosis unless there is superimposed infection
imaging: Persistent mass, hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, or endobronchial obstruction on chest x-ray or CT
Opacity that fails to improve after appropriate antibiotics
Tissue diagnosis by bronchoscopy or biopsy

differential.name: COVID-19 pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Fever, cough, dyspnea and bilateral opacities are indistinguishable from other viral pneumonias on clinical grounds alone.

history: Known exposure or outbreak setting
Anosmia or ageusia
Progressive dyspnea about a week after initial symptoms
exam: Hypoxemia that may be out of proportion to the degree of distress
Diffuse rather than focal lung findings
labs: SARS-CoV-2 PCR or antigen test positive
Lymphopenia and elevated D-dimer and CRP
imaging: Bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities on chest x-ray or CT
No lobar consolidation or air bronchograms typical of bacterial pneumonia

differential.name: Aspiration pneumonitis
differential.why_considered: Fever, cough, hypoxemia and a focal opacity after an aspiration event can look identical to aspiration pneumonia.

history: Clear episode of choking or vomiting followed by symptoms within hours
Impaired swallowing, sedation, alcohol or drug use
Symptoms may improve within 24 to 48 hours without antibiotics
exam: Focal crackles over the right lower or posterior upper lobe
Signs of dysphagia or reduced consciousness
labs: WBC may be normal or mildly elevated
imaging: Opacity in a dependent segment (right lower lobe or posterior upper lobe)
Rapid improvement on repeat imaging supports pneumonitis rather than infection

severity.mild: Afebrile or low-grade fever, mild cough, no dyspnea at rest, oxygen saturation 94% or higher on room air, able to eat and drink, no confusion; suitable for outpatient treatment.
severity.moderate: Fever, productive cough, dyspnea on exertion, tachypnea, focal crackles, oxygen saturation 90 to 94%, mild leukocytosis; often needs admission or close observation.
severity.severe: Marked dyspnea at rest, accessory muscle use, oxygen saturation below 90%, confusion, hypotension or rising BUN and lactate; requires inpatient care with oxygen and intravenous antibiotics.
severity.critical: Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, septic shock with vasopressors, or multiorgan dysfunction; managed in the intensive care unit.

red_flags.finding: Respiratory rate 30/min or higher or oxygen saturation below 90% on room air
red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory failure; needs immediate oxygen and admission

red_flags.finding: Confusion or new altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Hypoxemia, sepsis or central nervous system infection; a CURB-65 criterion and a poor prognostic sign

red_flags.finding: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg or diastolic 60 mm Hg or lower
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis with hypoperfusion; needs fluid resuscitation and vasopressor assessment
Septic shock physiology; urgent resuscitation and intensive care

red_flags.finding: Rising PaCO2 or falling pH on blood gas
red_flags.meaning: Respiratory muscle fatigue and impending ventilatory failure
Atypical or overwhelming infection; part of the Pneumonia Severity Index and a marker of severe disease

red_flags.finding: New atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis-related arrhythmia that can worsen hemodynamics

red_flags.finding: Failure to improve after 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Consider resistant organism, empyema, abscess, endocarditis, tuberculosis or malignancy

complications.name: Pleural effusion
clues: Persistent fever despite antibiotics
Stony dullness and decreased breath sounds at the base
Blunting of the costophrenic angle on chest x-ray

complications.name: Empyema
clues: High fever and pleuritic pain that persist
Loculated pleural fluid on CT or ultrasound
Pleural fluid pH below 7.2, glucose low, or frank pus

complications.name: Lung abscess
clues: Weeks of fever and productive cough
Cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level on imaging
Foul-smelling sputum suggesting anaerobes

complications.name: Bacteremia and septic shock
clues: Hypotension and tachycardia
Elevated lactate
Positive blood cultures

complications.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
clues: Rapidly worsening hypoxemia despite high-flow oxygen
Bilateral diffuse opacities not explained by effusion or cardiomegaly
Reduced lung compliance requiring mechanical ventilation

complications.name: Acute kidney injury
clues: Rising creatinine and BUN
Oliguria
Hypotension or nephrotoxic antibiotic exposure

complications.name: Post-obstructive or nonresolving pneumonia from an underlying malignancy
clues: Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe
Persistent opacity after adequate therapy
Weight loss and hemoptysis

special_populations.differences: Often viral and self-limited; fever, tachypnea and cough dominate, sputum is rarely produced, and abdominal pain or vomiting may be prominent. Chest x-ray is not required for outpatient management, and amoxicillin is first-line when bacterial pneumonia is suspected.

May show no specific respiratory signs; poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, vomiting or fever without a source may be the only clues. Tachypnea and retractions are the most reliable findings, and young infants often require admission.

Fever may be absent or blunted, and confusion, falls or functional decline may be the presenting complaint. Chest examination can be unimpressive despite significant infection, and mortality is higher.

Presentation is similar to non-pregnant adults, but physiologic dyspnea and fatigue can delay recognition. Hypoxemia develops faster and threatens both mother and fetus; chest ultrasound or a shielded chest x-ray is preferred, and treatment should not be delayed.

Fever may be blunted and symptoms insidious. Consider Pneumocystis jirovecii, fungi, mycobacteria and unusual organisms; hypoxemia may be out of proportion to chest x-ray findings, and bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage is often needed.
More severe illness and higher risk of bacteremia; fever and symptoms can be blunted, and hyperglycemia often worsens during infection and requires adjustment of therapy.
Antibiotic doses need adjustment and nephrotoxic agents should be avoided; elevated BUN and creatinine also worsen the CURB-65 and Pneumonia Severity Index scores.
Chest x-ray quality is often limited and hypoxemia may be more pronounced; weight-based antibiotic dosing and attention to positioning and ventilation are important.

key_questions.question: How long have you had the cough, and is it bringing anything up?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute onset over 1–3 days with productive cough; yellow, green or rust-colored sputum supports bacterial pneumonia

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever or chills, and how high did it get?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever 101–103°F with chills or rigors; a blunted or absent fever is common in older adults

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath, and is it worse with activity or at rest?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea on exertion or at rest; resting dyspnea suggests more severe disease and possible hypoxemia

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you take a deep breath or cough?
key_questions.looking_for: Sharp, focal pleuritic chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing

key_questions.question: Did this start after a cold or flu-like illness?
key_questions.looking_for: A few days of viral upper respiratory symptoms followed by worsening fever and productive cough

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea, vomiting or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Gastrointestinal symptoms can accompany pneumonia, especially in children and with atypical organisms

key_questions.question: Have you had any confusion, falls or a change in your usual level of function?
key_questions.looking_for: New confusion or functional decline, which may be the presenting feature in older adults and is a CURB-65 criterion

key_questions.question: Do you have any chronic lung, heart, kidney or liver disease, or diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that increase risk and severity and affect the Pneumonia Severity Index

key_questions.question: Have you been in the hospital, a nursing home or on a ventilator recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Healthcare exposure within 90 days raises concern for healthcare-associated or drug-resistant organisms

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble swallowing, or have you choked on food or liquids?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysphagia or aspiration risk from stroke, dementia or neuromuscular disease

key_questions.question: Do you take steroids, chemotherapy, a proton pump inhibitor or any medicine that weakens the immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppressive or aspiration-risk medications that broaden the differential and change management

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, or have you been around secondhand smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former smoking, a strong risk factor for pneumonia and for underlying lung disease

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy alcohol use, which increases risk of aspiration and severe pneumonia

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently, stayed in a hotel or cruise ship, or been around hot tubs or cooling systems?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposure to contaminated water aerosols suggesting Legionella

key_questions.question: Have you been around birds, poultry or farm animals?
key_questions.looking_for: Bird or animal exposure suggesting psittacosis or other zoonotic causes

key_questions.question: Have you had a cough for more than 3 weeks, coughed up blood, or lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic cough, hemoptysis or weight loss suggesting tuberculosis or malignancy rather than acute pneumonia

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a blood clot in your leg or lung, or recent surgery or immobility?
key_questions.looking_for: Venous thromboembolism risk that would make pulmonary embolism a competing diagnosis

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy must be excluded before chest x-ray or CT and affects antibiotic choice

key_questions.question: Have you had your pneumococcal or influenza vaccines?
key_questions.looking_for: Vaccination status, which modifies risk and supports prevention counseling

key_questions.question: Is anyone else at home or at work sick with a similar illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Clustering of respiratory illness suggesting a circulating viral infection

reasoning_points: Acute onset over 1–3 days of fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea
Focal inspiratory crackles, dullness to percussion, bronchial breath sounds or egophony on lung exam
Tachypnea, hypoxemia on pulse oximetry, and tachycardia supporting a lower respiratory infection
Leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance and a left shift on CBC
Chest x-ray showing a new focal airspace opacity or consolidation with air bronchograms
Severity assessed with CURB-65 or the Pneumonia Severity Index to guide site of care
Pregnancy excluded before chest imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Competing diagnoses such as pulmonary embolism, heart failure, acute bronchitis, tuberculosis and malignancy considered and addressed
Blood and sputum cultures obtained before antibiotics in severe disease or when resistant organisms are suspected
Complications such as pleural effusion, empyema, lung abscess, bacteremia and respiratory failure considered

easy: Young or middle-aged adult with a classic story of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain after a cold
Focal crackles and dullness over one lobe on auscultation and percussion
Chest x-ray with a clear lobar consolidation and air bronchograms
No significant comorbidities and normal oxygen saturation
medium: Older adult with a blunted fever and an unimpressive chest exam despite significant infection
Atypical presentation with dry cough, headache, malaise and diffuse or interstitial opacities
Overlap with acute decompensated heart failure in a patient with known cardiac disease
Mild hypoxemia and tachypnea requiring a decision about inpatient versus outpatient care
Recent antibiotic or healthcare exposure raising concern for a resistant organism
hard: Older adult presenting with confusion, a fall or functional decline and no fever or cough
Immunocompromised patient with insidious dry cough and hypoxemia out of proportion to the chest x-ray
Pregnant patient with dyspnea that could be physiologic or infectious
Pneumonia that fails to improve after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, suggesting empyema, abscess, tuberculosis or malignancy
Patient with a competing diagnosis such as pulmonary embolism, in whom the chest x-ray is normal or nonspecific
Infant or young child with fever, poor feeding and tachypnea but no localizing findings
